playbook:
**Playbook for ref_commons (shared fishery):**

- Early and middle seasons: submit exactly the stated sustainable share. Cooperation keeps the stock at max, which keeps every season's sustainable share high. In this run five seasons of matching the share held the stock at 100 throughout — the strategy works when others mirror it.
- If others start slightly overfishing (landed above the share), don't retaliate and don't chase them — stay at my sustainable share. The stock recovers fast (50% regrowth) and small defections barely hurt me.
- On the final season there is no future to protect: submit a large catch. The real cap is the remaining stock minus what others will take, minus a small buffer — not the sustainable share. Asking for ~70% of stock when others took ~11 each landed cleanly; I could likely go even closer to the full residual. The buffer guards against others also defecting big, so size it to the risk that they do.
- Watch the season counter: the temptation to defect one season early is not worth it — grabbing early drops the stock and lowers every remaining sustainable share, while defecting on the true final turn costs nothing.
- If others defect big mid-game (landed far above the share), reassess: stay cooperative only if the stock still recovers to near cap; if it's eroding, shift to taking my residual share before it's gone.
- Never let the stock approach zero before the final season; a finished fishery zeros all my remaining turns, which dwarfs any short-term gain.
- Final-season expectations: with 6 seasons of full cooperation I totalled ~115 (55.5 from steady shares + ~60 from the last-season grab). The last-season defection was worth about one extra full season — always take it.

1.text:
When I open a shared-stock game, my first move is to compute the exact sustainable catch per player and stay at it while the stock is at its maximum. Cooperative-adjacent play kept the stock at cap every season and my score accumulating steadily — that worked exactly as intended.

When the stock is at or near its cap, I submit exactly the sustainable share, not below it. Leaving fish under the share is pure loss when the stock can't grow past its ceiling anyway. Only fish under the share if the stock is depressed and I'm protecting recovery.

When I'm tempted to grab above the sustainable share mid-game, I should recognize the math: a modest over-catch gains ~2 fish once but drops the stock and invites rivals to reciprocate, likely costing me sustainable yield in later rounds. Net gain roughly zero plus added risk. So: no mid-game over-catching even if it looks free.

When rivals consistently land at or under the sustainable share, I match them exactly and free-ride on the stable stock. When any rival over-fishes, I still hold at sustainability unless the stock is clearly headed to collapse anyway.

On the final turn of a finite game, sustainability no longer matters — I take a larger catch (roughly 20% above the share) since there's no future to protect. This cost nothing: the stock stays well above zero and I banked ~2.4 extra fish. Keep this move.

One caution: verify the final round really is final before defecting. If the episode count or season total is uncertain, stay at the sustainable share — the upside from defecting is small and the downside of triggering a defection spiral in extra rounds is large.

Overall: hold the cooperative equilibrium through all but the last round, trust that others holding steady makes it pay, and defect only when the game is definitively about to end.

2.text:
My playbook for the fishery game:

- Early seasons: when the stock is at or near full and others are taking the sustainable share, I match the sustainable share exactly. This keeps the stock at maximum and preserves cooperation. This worked perfectly for five straight seasons in the episode just played.
- Cooperation can be stable: if every boat keeps to the sustainable share and the stock stays at max, do not "pre-emptively" defect mid-game. Any early deviation risks triggering a cycle of overfishing that costs more than the one-season gain.
- When a rival takes above sustainable and the stock dips slightly, I do not chase them for one season's marginal gain — it barely moves my total but risks triggering escalation. Revert to the sustainable share the following season while the stock is still healthy.
- Final season: since regrowth no longer matters, extract fully — take roughly the whole stock divided by the number of boats (or as much as I can get). Taking 33.3 of a 100 stock was right; anything less than my full share of what remains is fish left on the dock.
- Second-to-last season: consider whether a modest overshoot is worth it if the stock is high and the last-season regrowth from a slightly reduced stock is small — but only if it won't cause rivals to punish me in the final round. With a short horizon and stable cooperation, staying at sustainable until the final round was the safer, near-optimal play.
- If others overfish repeatedly, I still keep to sustainable while the stock is high, because the fishery only dies at zero; small over-extraction by one boat is survivable across a short horizon.
- General rule: discount the last round (extract fully), cooperate on all earlier rounds, and only deviate if a single-round gain clearly outweighs the compounding loss of stock across remaining seasons.
